item.title: India’s ‘Cockroach’ Moment
item.description:
For a while, it wasn’t clear where the protests that brought tens of thousands of young people onto streets across India over the past month were going. The police had cracked down with force; the protesters were holding their ground in their campaign against the failures of the country’s education system and their own poor job prospects. It looked like things could potentially turn even uglier in the world’s largest democracy.

Then, over the weekend, the government blinked. Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s education minister resigned, meeting a key protester demand. The demonstrations have been called off, for now.

But that doesn’t mean the government’s problems with India’s young people are over. Today, Anupreeta Das, a South Asia correspondent who has been covering the protests, writes about India’s challenge to improve life for its vast population of people under 30. If it can’t, the country risks squandering their potential, with lasting consequences.

By Anupreeta Das

Narendra Modi almost never caves to anyone. But he caved to India’s young people.

This weekend, Modi capitulated to protesters’ demands that his education minister resign. It was an unexpected move by a strongman leader who isn’t fond of dissent; that he did so is an indication that Modi knows India’s youths have real power. They might not be able to improve their own lives at the moment — that’s why they’re protesting, after all — but they can at least make Modi’s life harder.

India’s massive young population is supposed to be one of its most important assets, with the potential to pay a big “demographic dividend,” as experts call it, if Modi plays his cards right. The high ratio of workers to retirees could help fuel the country’s productivity well into the period when countries like China begin to stagger under the weight of their aging populations.

But on its current path, India may well end up squandering its demographic advantages. Critics say the country’s education system is mismanaged, youth unemployment rates are high, and the bureaucracy is sclerotic. Gender disparities persist in schools and workplaces, and the instability that results from a large informal labor force hinders growth.

That’s a problem for Modi and a problem for India’s future. Because as the recent protests have shown, if India doesn’t figure out how to create more jobs for its young people, the demographics that were supposed to pay dividends could wind up fueling instability.

India’s Gen Z protests?

For many observers, India’s protests brought to mind the Gen Z uprisings that unfolded in multiple countries across the world, including in India’s backyard, where student revolts in Bangladesh and Nepal brought down governments.

Such an outcome was always unlikely in a country as diverse and vast as India, whose 28 states each have their own issues, making a truly united movement tough to pull off.

Still, the protests over the past month were nationwide. And the challenge the Indian government is facing is the same one faced by Bangladesh and Nepal. It needs to build an economy that can create jobs at roughly the same rate as people are entering the work force.

The student-led protests were a response, most directly, to two events: a disparaging remark in May by India’s top judge, comparing India’s unemployed youths to “cockroaches,” and the cancellation of a highly competitive medical college-entrance test after the discovery that exam questions had been leaked.

Those catalysts were insults that added to longstanding injuries. Anger over the cancellation of the exam reflected broader concerns about the intense pressure within India’s higher education system, where millions compete for seats often allocated to a few hundred thousand. (In May, 2.2 million students sat for the medical school exam that was canceled, competing for roughly 140,000 seats.)

And anger about the “cockroaches” remark unfolded in an environment where competition for jobs is fierce. In 2022, 10 million people competed for 35,000 railway jobs, according to the state-owned Indian Railways. A widely cited 2026 study by Azim Premji University found that nearly 40 percent of graduates between the ages of 15 and 25 were unemployed. One student who learned of the judge’s remark founded the satirically named Cockroach Janta Party, which spearheaded this month’s protests.

Youth, power and “Developed India”

The median age in India is 29, and more than 40 percent of Indians — around 600 million — are under 25. The vast majority of the population is between the ages of 15 and 64, in their most productive years.

These numbers provide an opportunity for economic growth and development, but they won’t pay dividends unless the right policies are in place to give India’s young people a fair shot at becoming skilled, educated and productive workers.

Modi himself has often said that India’s youths are the source of its power. He speaks of India’s favorable population dynamics when pitching his “Vikshit Bharat,” or “Developed India,” vision to voters. India’s young will drive the country’s transformation to an economically prosperous and well-governed global power by 2047, the 100th anniversary of India’s independence, Modi likes to say.

And so it was unusual to see protests on this scale from a generation that has been brought up believing that India’s time has come and that Modi is the man to take it into the future. Many people I spoke to during the demonstrations said they felt let down by the prime minister, that his promises had yet to be fulfilled, but because of his heavy-handed approach to criticism, few had been willing to stand up to him — until now.

Modi acted quickly to appoint a billionaire Indian tech czar, Nandan Nilekani, to lead the overhaul of the education system — a signal to young people that their prime minister is listening. But that’s only a small piece of the accountability they’re demanding. As the protests wrapped up, I heard two lines of thought. The optimists felt they’d laid a solid foundation for bringing about lasting change. The pessimists felt that, as students went back to their daily lives, governance would continue as before. Should that happen, they said, they were prepared to act again.

Firefighters in Spain and France raced to contain raging fires yesterday ahead of another heat wave that is forecast to push temperatures above 40 degrees Celsius and strong winds that could spark new blazes. Officials said it was already the region’s worst wildfire season in modern history.

Fires around the cities of Bordeaux, in France, and Madrid and Valencia in Spain have been fueled by parched vegetation after weeks of heat waves. In France, firefighters encountered a fire-fueled thunderstorm known as a “fire cloud,” which produces lightning and burning embers that can spark more fires, and high winds that could spread them.

See photos and videos of the fires.

Madrid is booming, culturally and economically. However, the proximity of the wildfires is a suffocating reality check — a possible harbinger for the damage to come as the continent warms.

With firefighters stretched thin, residents in France’s evacuation zones are putting themselves at risk, using water tanks, hoses and tractors to save homes.

Saudi Arabia blamed Iran-backed Iraqi militias for drone attacks on its petroleum facilities. The kingdom is being dragged deeper into the wider regional conflict as it faces attacks from Iraq and Yemen.

OnlyFans is a site best known for its adult content. But a team of American scientists, trying to raise money to offset government budget cuts, is using the platform for something more wholesome: They’re uploading videos of wild marmots. On the account, OnlyMarms, viewers can find G-rated “marmot content,” which shows the squirrel-like rodents burrowing into nests or scurrying across rocks.

Karyna Shuliak, the girlfriend of Jeffrey Epstein, the notorious sex offender, is a complicated figure. A 37-year-old dentist, she was the last person Epstein called before he killed himself in his jail cell in 2019. She also stands to inherit as much as $100 million from his estate.

The release of the Epstein files put Shuliak and Epstein’s nearly eight-year relationship on vivid display. They fought about sex and jetted around the world together. She had free use of a credit card. And over the years, she began to help manage his properties and staff. Here’s what we know about Shuliak and her relationship with Epstein.

Tā moko is a ritual body art practiced by the Māori, New Zealand’s Indigenous inhabitants. The craft was traditionally handed down from parent to child, but after it was banned under British colonial rule, the Māori people began hiding their tattoos and stopped teaching the practice to younger generations.

More than a century later, the facial tattoos known as moko kanohi are once again visible on the streets and in the halls of Parliament. Young Māori have taken to documenting their tā moko ceremonies on social media. And some have even persuaded their elders to be tattooed. Read more about the tā moko revival.

It is classic Alpine fare, taken straight from the chef’s childhood in Zurich. The rolled oats are golden with brown sugar and a hint of maple, with salt and a wisp of olive oil for depth.

item.title: World’s Biggest Crypto Exchange Has Made It Harder to Fight Crime, Police Say
item.description:
Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, has quietly changed how it cooperates with law enforcement in many countries around the world, frustrating investigators who say the company has made it harder to find scammers and combat money laundering.

The new policy is a big shift for Binance. The company had tried to clean up its act after years of legal problems, working directly with investigators to freeze suspicious accounts and share information about customers making fishy transactions.

But in April of last year, Binance enacted a policy requiring law enforcement officials to route certain requests to foreign government agencies, a time-consuming process governed by international treaties. That rule, along with an exodus of a group of senior compliance employees, has stymied some investigations in Europe and raised concerns in the United States, The New York Times found.

Binance moves billions of dollars in digital coins every day, leading a booming global industry that has been embraced by the Trump administration. Last year, President Trump eased federal scrutiny on crypto companies at the same time that his family’s crypto start-up forged a business relationship with Binance.

The company said that it had not slowed its cooperation with law enforcement, and that the change was meant to ensure that Binance followed regulations and privacy laws when handling customers’ personal data. There is no indication that the change was related to the Trump administration’s easing of regulations.

But investigators said the policy had created new obstacles for fighting financial crime.

Police officers from five European countries who attended a law enforcement conference in the Netherlands last month said they struggled to get information from Binance, except in cases involving child sexual abuse materials, terrorism or an imminent threat to life. A senior European law enforcement official said that most requests had been channeled to the government of the United Arab Emirates, where Binance is regulated, dramatically slowing response times.

In the United States, law enforcement is largely exempt from the requirement to submit requests to foreign governments, said three people with knowledge of the policy. But in some cases, Binance asks state prosecutors to route their requests through other countries, which has hindered at least two investigations this year, according to people familiar with the cases as well as messages reviewed by The Times.

Alona Katz, an assistant district attorney in Brooklyn, told The Times that she generally had found Binance to be responsive, sometimes providing information within hours. But she said she was unable to obtain account records from some Binance users based in the United Arab Emirates.

In fast-moving cases, when criminals move funds between accounts in minutes or even seconds, speed is of the essence to recover stolen funds, she said. “How fast you get your records determines the outcome of your case,” she said. “It’s everything.”

“For the sake of victims of crypto theft, it is important to have the timely and forthcoming cooperation from these massive, and highly profitable, cryptocurrency corporations,” Alvin Bragg, the Manhattan district attorney, said in a statement.

Binance offers a gateway for ordinary people to buy cryptocurrency. It has also struggled to root out crime. The company paid $4.3 billion in penalties to the U.S. government after pleading guilty in 2023 to compliance violations that allowed hackers, swindlers and other criminals to move money. The company’s billionaire founder, Changpeng Zhao, spent four months in federal prison.

Under its plea deal with the Justice Department, Binance agreed to take steps to prevent financial crime. While most crypto transactions are recorded on a public ledger, funds that enter an exchange such as Binance are impossible to trace, unless the company turns over information about an account.

Got a confidential news tip? The New York Times would like to hear from readers who want to share messages and materials with our journalists.

Even before the deal was finalized, Binance began cooperating enthusiastically with law enforcement, including turning over the identities of account holders, according to officials in Europe and the United States. The company built a staff of hundreds of compliance officers, many of them veterans of U.S. and European law enforcement agencies. The police could often get information about accounts far faster from Binance than they could from banks.

Since Mr. Trump was inaugurated in early 2025, his administration has taken a much friendlier approach to the crypto industry than its predecessor did. Binance has forged business ties with World Liberty Financial, the crypto company founded by the president and his sons. The Emirati venture firm MGX used a World Liberty cryptocurrency to buy a stake in Binance, a major boost to the Trump start-up. And in a memo in April 2025, Todd Blanche, now the acting attorney general, said the administration would stop targeting exchanges such as Binance and focus on prosecuting criminals who abused the platforms. Mr. Trump also pardoned Mr. Zhao.

Late last year, Binance fired or suspended several of its top compliance employees. The officials had sounded alarms about $1.7 billion that they said had flowed from Binance accounts to Iranian entities. Binance has disputed the employees’ findings and said that they were not disciplined for raising compliance concerns. Several other senior compliance officials left around the same time.

That shake-up meant some investigators and prosecutors lost their main points of contact at Binance, according to people familiar with the matter. And the exit of so many senior members of the compliance staff has led to confusion within the company about how to deal with law enforcement requests.

The rules that Binance introduced in April 2025 are complex and so far have had more severe consequences for investigators in Europe.

There, Binance now often requires law enforcement officials who want information about accounts outside their home country — a German prosecutor seeking to freeze the account of someone in Asia, for example — to follow procedures laid out in mutual legal assistance treaties, agreements that govern how countries share information in law enforcement investigations. (The same agreements apply to banks.)

Noah Perlman, the chief compliance officer for Binance, said that “in some cross-border cases, foreign law enforcement may be directed to the appropriate formal legal process.”

Still, he said, the company had increased its cooperation with law enforcement “while navigating the increasing complexity of governments as they seek to regulate crypto and data protection.” When law enforcement agencies seek information about accounts in their own countries, Binance works with them directly. The company has gone “far beyond” its legal obligation, Mr. Perlman said, and remains committed to fulfilling the requirements of its 2023 settlement with the United States.

But concerns have persisted. In December, Binance gained a license to operate in Abu Dhabi. Since then, certain information requests flow through the Emirati government, raising concerns among current and former law enforcement officials. They argue that the Emiratis have a conflict of interest, because the investment firm MGX is funded by Abu Dhabi royals.

Mr. Perlman said there was no conflict of interest. A spokeswoman for Binance’s regulator in Abu Dhabi said it was committed to protecting market integrity and countering financial crime. MGX did not respond to a request for comment.

This spring, U.S. investigators began to worry that the company’s rules would become more cumbersome, mirroring what was taking place in Europe.

A Binance compliance official informed the Justice Department that starting on June 8, the company would extend its treaty requirement to cover a wider range of American law enforcement requests, three people familiar with the matter said. Around the same time, top officials in the Justice Department sent an email to prosecutors warning that Binance was about to dial back its cooperation, according to The Information.

The company’s top executives did not move forward with that plan, the people said. Ms. Katz, the Brooklyn prosecutor, said that if it were to happen, it would be “devastating for our victims.”

item.title: What to Know About the Kumamoto Earthquake in Japan
item.description:
A powerful 6.8 magnitude earthquake struck southwestern Japan on Tuesday afternoon, damaging buildings and homes, igniting fires and injuring dozens, prompting a search for people who may have been trapped in rubble.

Here’s what to know.

The earthquake hit around 4:30 p.m. local time in Kumamoto Prefecture on Kyushu island, the southernmost of Japan’s main islands.

The earthquake’s intensity led to buildings collapsing in the region. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi of Japan said people were trapped inside some structures. Fires also erupted in Kumamoto City, the regional capital, which has a population of more than 700,000.

The epicenter of the quake was near Uto, a smaller coastal city around 30 miles south of Kumamoto City, according to the U.S. Geological Survey

The U.S. agency had earlier reported a magnitude measurement of 7.1 for the earthquake before it adjusted the figure to 6.8.

View the location of the quake’s epicenter and shake area.

The second floor of a shopping mall in southern Kumamoto City collapsed, injuring two people. Crews were working to rescue people who may have been trapped inside. Video footage posted on social media showed debris scattered inside and outside the mall.

Aerial footage showed a flipped train carriage on tracks in the city and widespread damage to buildings and bridges. Other images recorded by the public broadcaster NHK also captured elevated sections of the Kyushu Expressway that had split into two pieces, as other footage showed a wall that had partly collapsed at Kumamoto Castle, a landmark in the city’s center.

The prime minister said the authorities were still assessing the severity of the damage to buildings and bridges.

At least one person died in a hospital after being found in a collapsed house in Kumamoto, according to the police.

At least 50 people were being treated for injuries at a hospital in Hikawa, a town to the south of Kumamoto City, according to NHK.

The last major quake in Japan in 2024, centered on the Noto peninsula farther north, killed hundreds of people, with more succumbing to disaster-linked causes afterward, according to NHK.

In April 2016, the Kumamoto region also experienced days of deadly seismic events that killed at least nine and injured hundreds, according to the U.S. Geological Survey.

The Sendai Nuclear Power Plant appeared to be secure and had no reports of abnormalities, Minoru Kihara, a top Japanese cabinet official, said during a news briefing.

The power plant, which has two reactors and supplies electricity to the Kyushu region, is in Kagoshima, south of Kumamoto.

item.title: How Cubans Are Surviving
item.description:
Why hasn’t Cuba’s government collapsed yet? It’s been six months since President Trump cut off the island’s fuel sources, in an effort to force political change. “It’s just going to fall,” he told reporters on Jan. 4. And yet, it hasn’t.

The New York Times recently sent a team of journalists to Cuba to try to figure out why. (It’s highly unusual for the Cuban government to grant Times journalists visas to report from the island. The last time was almost eight years ago.)

What they found was a remarkable story of people adapting to extreme circumstances — with lithium batteries, jury-rigged generators, solar panels and more. My colleague Sam Sifton, who hosts our sister newsletter, The Morning, spoke with our reporter Jack Nicas about his recent trip, and what it took to report from Cuba.

Sam: I want to ask you about one farmer you met who devised a tiny backyard refinery to make gasoline out of shredded plastic. “Cubans thrive amid crisis,” he told you. Did you see a lot of that kind of ingenuity in Cuba?

Jack: One of the most important words in the Cuban lexicon is “resolver.” It literally means “to solve,” but in Cuba, after decades of a U.S. trade embargo, it really means “to figure things out by any means necessary.”

It explains how Cubans put Soviet engines into 1950s American cars to keep them running or ate breaded grapefruit rinds to imitate meat during their economic crisis following the fall of the Soviet Union.

And now they’re resolviendo again. We saw a lot of creativity during our trip across Cuba. People drilled solar panels to the tops of electric rickshaws. They are using lithium batteries to power concerts. There are even stories of people powering their cars with charcoal and cooking oil.

As a result, the country is still functioning, despite the hardship.

Sam: What was your reception in the country like? It’s been a long time since the Cuban government has allowed Times journalists to report there.

Jack: Everywhere we turned there were stories, and the Cuban people were eager to tell them. We spoke to dozens of people in Havana and beyond who wanted to express their frustration and exhaustion with the status quo. It was a mixed bag on whom they blamed. Some saw the Cuban government at fault for failed economic policies and political repression, while others believed Trump was making them suffer for his own personal gain. Many blamed both.

Sam: How hard was it to get your visa? Did government minders follow you around?

Jack: It took a lot of convincing to get. I met with top Cuban diplomats in Mexico City, Havana, Washington and New York over six months, and sent many letters to persuade them that we would tell this story fairly. Once we got to Havana to report, we met with Cuban officials a few times, but they otherwise didn’t bother us. We traveled around freely, decided our story targets and chose whom we interviewed.

Read the team’s first dispatch from Cuba here.

Trump enjoys bringing world leaders into the Oval Office and letting news photographers and reporters capture him as he does it. But yesterday, he kept two meetings — one with Benjamin Netanyahu, the Israeli prime minister, and the other with Volodymyr Zelensky, the Ukrainian president — behind closed doors.

Trump and Netanyahu are each facing electoral challenges in the months ahead as their interests appear to be diverging sharply on the war with Iran. As for Trump and Zelensky, their relationship appears stronger than ever. Zelensky said they had discussed Trump’s pledge to allow Ukraine to produce U.S.-designed Patriot air defense systems.

Call him the Picasso of pointe shoes. Tim Foster sprays and daubs hundreds of shoes each season for New York City Ballet, turning standard-issue pale pink into a rainbow of hues. It’s a delicate, painstaking art: He must match costume colors exactly, so that the footwear doesn’t break the continuous line of the leg. “It has to be right,” he said, “because it’s their sacred tool. It’s their violin. It’s their oboe.”

Samosas in India. Noodles in South Korea. Papaya salad in Thailand. Across Asia, people are discovering that dishes that were once reliably cheap are no longer so affordable, as the shock waves of the war in Iran spread around the world.

Many Asian countries rely heavily on energy imports from the Middle East. Since the fighting began in February, their currencies have plummeted while inflation and prices of ingredients have surged. Customers and food sellers alike are feeling the pinch. “We are all in the same boat, hoping it won’t sink,” said one Bangkok street food vendor. Read more about how war makes noodles more expensive.

There’s no overstating how important seals are to Greenland. They’ve provided sustenance for centuries in an environment where it’s difficult to survive. People there eat seals, feed them to their sled dogs and use their bones for jewelry. The sealskin trade is a major business, providing income for thousands of Inuit hunters.

My colleagues visited the Great Greenland tannery in the southern town of Qaqortoq to see how pelts are turned into clothing. It isn’t easy. Take a look.

item.title: Houthis Claim Strike on Another Saudi Oil Tanker
item.description:
The Iranian-backed Houthi militant group in Yemen said on Tuesday that it had targeted a Saudi oil tanker with missiles in what would be the latest attack in an emerging front of the war between the United States and Iran.

The skirmishes between the Houthis, who control a large part of Yemen, and the Saudis risked igniting another conflict and infused more volatility into world energy supplies.

Saudi authorities did not immediately confirm the attack on the latest tanker, the NCC Ghazal, which is listed by public maritime monitoring services as Saudi-flagged. The ship was last located five days ago, along Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea coast, by MarineTraffic, a ship-monitoring firm.

The Houthis said the tanker ignored repeated warnings and was forced to reverse course. They did not say if the ship was actually hit, or where the vessel was at the time.

It was at least the fourth oil tanker to be attacked since the militia announced that it would blockade shipping to and from Saudi Arabia in the Red Sea. A monitoring group run by the British navy said, hours after the Houthi claim, that a tanker heard an explosion while transiting the Red Sea and all crew members were safe.

Shortly after the Houthis claimed the attack, the Saudi ministry of defense said that for the second consecutive day, it had destroyed several drones launched by Iran-aligned militias in Iraq aimed at Saudi oil facilities.

Since the Houthis announced their blockade earlier this month, each side has claimed attacks on the other. A Saudi-led military coalition has carried out airstrikes in Houthi-held territory for the first time in years. Separate from shipping attacks, the Houthis on Monday said they had targeted crude oil supplies and transport routes linking Saudi Arabia’s eastern oil fields to the Red Sea hub of Yanbu. The kingdom’s defense ministry has not yet addressed that claim.

Since March, Iran has effectively blockaded the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow portal to the Persian Gulf. That has forced Saudi Arabia to rely more heavily on exporting oil and gas through its Red Sea ports, hundreds of miles away.

The Houthis control most of Yemen’s Red Sea coast, where the southern part of the sea narrows to meet the Bab al-Mandab Strait — the link to the Indian Ocean and the shortest route to Asian markets. If ships cannot use that passage, they must instead go north through the Suez Canal, adding thousands of miles to some voyages.

In the last week, the Houthis claimed attacks on two tankers in the Red Sea, only one of which Saudi Arabia confirmed. Later, on Friday, the hull of a Saudi-owned vessel was damaged after being targeted in the Red Sea, Saudi officials said.

The Houthis form part of Iran’s broader “axis of resistance” alongside Iraqi factions, Hamas in Gaza and Hezbollah in Lebanon. With Iranian backing, they fought a civil war against the Saudi-backed, internationally recognized government of Yemen, taking over a swath of the country.

While the Saudis and the Houthis have been in a fragile stalemate since a cease-fire in 2022, tensions erupted this month when the Houthis accused Saudi Arabia of striking Yemen’s main international airport in Sanaa, the capital, in a dispute over an Iranian plane that tried to land there. The Houthis retaliated by attacking the Abha airport in southern Saudi Arabia, the first direct Houthi strike on Saudi soil since early 2022.

The Houthis have weaponized their ability to disrupt shipping in the Red Sea before.

During the war in Gaza, which began in late 2023, the Houthis attacked commercial shipping in the Red Sea with drones, missiles and hijacking, trying to exert pressure on Israel and its allies. By some estimates, a Houthi blockade could affect more than 3 percent of the global oil market.

The latest Houthi threats come at a particularly difficult time, with Iran’s attacks on ships transiting the Strait of Hormuz prompting many shipowners and operators to decide it is too dangerous to use that waterway. The strait has been practically at a standstill, with the exception of a brief cease-fire, since the United States and Israel launched strikes on Iran on Feb. 28, and the number of crossings has hit some of its lowest levels in months.

item.title: Cut Off From Fuel, Cuba Is Still Surviving
item.description:
For months, President Trump has been predicting that Cuba is about to collapse.

“It’s just going to fall,” he told reporters on Jan. 4, a day after taking control of Venezuela’s oil, which had been Cuba’s lifeline.

He then imposed an oil blockade that has pushed the island into its worst ever energy crisis, with mass blackouts now lasting nearly all day. And yet, more than six months later, the Cuban government and people are still standing.

This month, we visited the country to understand how. After a week on the ground, we found that while Cubans are clearly suffering, they are also doing what perhaps they do best: adapting.

They are swapping their gas-guzzling 1950s American cars for electric motorcycles and rickshaws from China; importing hefty lithium batteries to keep televisions and fans running through blackouts; jury-rigging generators to run on more accessible natural gas; and installing solar panels on rooftops and even vehicles.

Together, the workarounds amount to a new Cuban energy grid — this one more in the hands of the Cuban people, propping up society with the electricity off and fuel lines dry.

These solutions have enabled the Cuban government to ration power by turning on the lights for just a few hours a day, stretching out whatever scarce fuel it has left in an effort to withstand Washington’s intense pressure campaign.

The result is that Cuba has lasted far longer without fuel shipments than the Trump administration appears to have expected.

Over nearly seven decades of U.S. pressure, Cuba has defied the odds and improvised to survive. Now it seems that Mr. Trump, like many U.S. presidents before him, is also finding that toppling the government founded by Fidel Castro is not so simple.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters last week that the Trump administration still wants to see the Cuban government fall. “We’re prepared to be very realistic about how you do that, and patient,” he said. “These are complex things that take time, and obviously we’re prepared to do what we can.”

The Cuban government is seeking a deal. “Cuba is not an enemy of the United States,” Carlos Fernández de Cossio, Cuba’s deputy foreign minister, said in an interview. “What we would like is a constructive and respectful relationship.”

Meantime, the Cuban people, as they have for decades, are making do. “Cubans thrive amid crisis,” said Humberto Palmero, a 55-year-old farmer, standing on the hill where he grew up along Cuba’s coastline, with a view toward Florida. His siblings had already left for Miami and his two children are fleeing to Spain, but he said he is determined to stay.

After hearing about the oil blockade, Mr. Palmero learned on YouTube how to distill junk plastic into homemade gasoline and diesel. He has since built a tiny, makeshift refinery in his backyard to power his motorcycle and light his stove.

“We look for solutions,” he said. “The economic restrictions are slowly killing us, but we’re pulling through with all our might, managing to get by until we see what happens next.”

In Havana and beyond, the crisis’s effects were clear.

We met families walking two hours for water because government pumps had run out of diesel. Women, lacking gas, cooked with firewood on the street. Powerless refrigerators became cabinets. Hitchhikers littered roadsides after the city halted public busing. And dozens of people told us they were simply exhausted after so many sleepless nights in the sweltering heat without fans or air-conditioning.

But we also saw a country that was still functioning.

Vehicles were on the road — despite black-market gasoline reaching $30 a gallon — because many were electric. Restaurants were open for the few who could afford them, powered by rumbling generators out back. Hospitals, government buildings and the airport had power because they were on protected parts of the grid. Medical clinics, nursing homes and bank branches ran off solar panels donated by China.

Cell service was sometimes working. Televisions showing the World Cup were not hard to find. And even roadside stands were serving cold beer from refrigerators powered by the sun.

But the makeshift energy grid also exposed Cuba’s inequality.

The batteries, solar panels and electric vehicles overwhelmingly belong to wealthier Cubans, which usually means those with relatives abroad. Their poorer neighbors often live without power and scrape by with meager pay amid rising inflation.

“The situation here is fine, because the owner can afford to buy solar panels,” said Yeny Oliva, 26, a bartender at a roadside restaurant. “But for us, at home, life is awful.” On wages of roughly $1 a day, she said, she struggles to buy milk for her 3-year-old daughter, and then their food spoils quickly without electricity.

Yet she also was grateful for the solar energy. Without power, the restaurant had closed. Then, the owners installed the panels and she was back at work.

While not everyone can afford alternative power sources, their energy has trickled down. Electric rickshaws ferry people to work. Solar panels have kept stores open. And people charge their phones and lanterns off their neighbor’s battery or the generator at work.

In one neighborhood, we saw one of the few families with a generator set up a television in the street so children could watch cartoons.

“We have not reached the point of having a humanitarian crisis precisely because of the strength of our society,” Mr. Fernández de Cossio, Cuba’s deputy foreign minister, said in Havana’s Fidel Castro museum, where the lights were on but the air-conditioning had failed. “The intimate expectation in political circles in the United States was that Cuba could not survive beyond April. And here we are.”

Other than a single Russian oil tanker in March, allies have not been willing to test Washington’s effective oil blockade.

As a result, Cuba has been powering its electric grid solely with domestic oil and gas and a growing network of solar parks sponsored by China. Together, they are enough to support roughly half of Cuban demand, according to Jorge Piñón, who studies Cuban energy at the University of Texas.

To preserve that supply, the government strategically cuts power at certain times and in certain places. It also runs plants at lower capacity to keep them from failing; extracts more natural gas; and even tries to refine sludgy oil residues from the bottom of years-old tanks.

“They are literally scraping the bottom of the barrel,” Mr. Piñón said.

Mr. Piñón said he and other analysts underestimated the Cuban government’s resourcefulness when they forecast it would exhaust its fuel stocks by March. But now he is skeptical of the government’s claim in May that the island has run out of fuel. On our trip, it was clear gasoline and diesel were still circulating.

At least some is coming from the United States. The Trump administration has allowed limited fuel exports to private businesses in Cuba, which has relieved pressure on black-market gas prices. And last week, the U.S. government’s first batch of $100 million in aid arrived.

The moves show how the Trump administration is exerting power over Cuba, ordering other nations to halt fuel shipments but allowing its own, and then providing aid in response to the resulting crisis. A White House spokeswoman said the Trump administration viewed Cuba as a threat to national security.

Exhausted Cubans told us they were angry at both Havana and Washington. Yet no one said they planned to take to the streets. Aside from banging pots and pans, the Cuban people have hardly staged protests.

“You go out to express your opinion on the street, and they throw you in jail or fine you,” said David Hechavarría Gamboa, 24, standing alongside his wife on a darkened street. “I can’t put my family at risk.”

When U.S. forces captured Venezuela’s leader, Nicolás Maduro, in January, Nelson Vega knew Cuba had a problem. Venezuelan oil had powered Cuba for years.

A month later, Mr. Vega, a 38-year-old entrepreneur, borrowed money from relatives in Florida to buy a Chinese-made electric rickshaw for $4,850. It took 10 hours to charge, and almost immediately, the blackouts made that difficult. So he invested a further $600 to drill solar panels to its roof.

Now he can power the entire battery by parking it in the sun for a day. “To me, this is the future,” he said. “We’re going to overcome the U.S. blockade.”

Once we traveled outside Havana, solar panels proliferated. Cuba’s power grid has been decaying in rural areas for years, making blackouts — and solar panels — already common.

On the road west, we met Abel Menéndez on a roof blanketed in panels. He has been selling and installing solar kits for five years, he said, but now both supply and demand have skyrocketed. At the same time, costs have dropped, to about $400 a panel from $500 a year earlier. “People are constantly calling,” he said.

We also came across a new field of panels — one of the government’s 54 solar parks, most inaugurated since 2025 and all built with China’s help.

Few countries are adopting solar faster than Cuba. Solar energy can now meet roughly 10 percent of Cuba’s electricity needs, the government says, up from 3 percent at the start of 2025. Cuban officials aim to depend fully on renewable energy by 2050.

For now, solar provides a boost, but it hardly solves Cuba’s problem. The island lacks the massive batteries needed to store solar power. That means it can provide roughly 20 percent of Cuba’s electricity at midday, but virtually none after the sun sets, during peak demand.

Perhaps Cuba’s hottest product of the moment are portable lithium batteries that can be charged in a few hours and then temporarily power televisions, fans or even refrigerators.

The most popular model costs about $750 in Cuba, sold on social media by Cubans who have imported them from China. That is more than most Cubans make in a year, so most of the batteries are sponsored by relatives abroad.

Other Cubans are electrifying their homes with the gas piped in for cooking and heating water. About 280,000 residences in Havana have such gas lines, and many are connecting them to modified generators designed to run on liquid fuel. Cuba produces the gas domestically, so it is one of the few energy sources not affected by the blockade.

The gas is also cheap, especially for the 120,000 households that pay a flat rate regardless of use. One man said he had been running a generator off gas almost nonstop, and yet was still billed the same 50 pesos, or eight cents, for the month.

On one of our final nights in Havana, we found a bar still full of patrons past midnight, powering its string lights and Latin music with a natural gas generator. Outside, we met Kiké Rodríguez, 37, founder of a Cuban barbecue business, Manteca, that has expanded during the crisis. He now employs 18 people to cook and deliver pork and plantains to customers across Havana.

“We’re the masters of this,” he said. “We’ve been figuring things out our whole lives.”

He pointed to the rooftop, where he said he was finishing a remodel to open his first brick-and-mortar restaurant, powered by the same generator.

“How are things going to play out? Nobody knows,” he added. “But when people say the country is going to fall apart, I don’t exactly know what they mean.”

I just spent a week in Cuba reporting on the energy crisis there. It was the first time in nearly eight years that the Cuban government let in staff from The New York Times to report. This story tells part of what I found there: Cubans are adapting to life with little fuel and electricity. We have more stories and videos rolling out this week.But what else do you want to know? I’ll be answering your questions here today.

Diana Karla Hernández and Dariel Pradas contributed reporting. Yasu Tsuji contributed video editing and production.

]]>

item.title: Fresh Clashes Erupt in Pakistani Kashmir on First Day of Contested Vote
item.description:
Fresh clashes erupted in the Pakistan-administered portion of Kashmir on Monday, the latest flare-up in weeks of violence that have left dozens dead and cast a shadow over a regional election underway in the Himalayan territory.

Thousands of supporters of a civil rights group, the Joint Awami Action Committee, or J.A.A.C., had gathered in Rawalakot, a town about 20 miles from the heavily militarized de facto border dividing regions of Kashmir claimed by India and Pakistan. Clashes broke out with the police on Rawalakot’s outskirts as the supporters tried to march toward Muzaffarabad, the regional capital.

The J.A.A.C. said that several of its supporters had died in clashes with the police, though the claim could not be independently verified and officials had not confirmed any deaths as of Tuesday.

Protesters in Kashmir have staged sit-ins, strikes and demonstrations since early June, calling for electoral reform ahead of the regional parliamentary election that began Monday and is scheduled to unfold in three phases until Aug. 10. The J.A.A.C.’s leadership and its supporters want to reallocate parliamentary seats reserved for Kashmiris living elsewhere in Pakistan to those who actually live in Kashmir — a move that Pakistan’s government has rejected, in part by arguing that it would require a constitutional reform.

J.A.A.C., a grass roots coalition of businessmen, students and civil society activists, has in the past campaigned for subsidized food prices and an end to financial advantages given to elected representatives in Kashmir. Protests also turned deadly in previous years, including in 2024 and 2025, although the current episode appears to be the deadliest since J.A.A.C.’s founding in 2023.

At least 30 people, including protesters, law enforcement personnel and bystanders, have died in clashes since early June and before Monday’s latest round of violence, according to local officials and independent estimates. Kashmir’s local government banned J.A.A.C. under antiterrorism laws days before a planned protest in June.

Umar Nazir Kashmiri, a senior J.A.A.C. leader, said in video messages on Monday that the movement was peaceful and that its leadership had instructed supporters not to carry weapons. He said the group still planned on marching to Muzaffarabad.

The police in Kashmir confirmed the clashes but did not say if there were fatalities. In a statement, they said two officers had been wounded by gunfire on Monday from what they described as “armed mobs.”

The New York Times could not independently verify the casualty figures or the sequence of events, because roads into Rawalakot, which is 40 miles away from Pakistan’s capital, Islamabad, are blocked and internet services across Kashmir have been suspended since June 5, severely restricting access to the area.

A senior administrative official in Rawalakot, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity around the protests, said that authorities had not yet confirmed any deaths because no bodies had been received in nearby hospitals.

The J.A.C.C. shifted its focus away from economic governance and to the region’s political system this year. It is now campaigning to abolish the allocation of 12 of Kashmir’s 45 assembly seats to refugees from India-administered Kashmir living across Pakistan.

Defenders of the provision say that the seats give displaced Kashmiris a legitimate voice in regional affairs. But the J.A.A.C. says non-Kashmiri political parties have leveraged those seats to influence or unseat local governments, and it has called for a boycott of the election.

The unrest in Kashmir is one of many crises hitting Pakistan, a country of 250 million where the powerful military is battling two insurgencies in the southern and western provinces of Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa that have killed thousands of security personnel in recent years.

item.title: Ukraine’s Strike on an Iranian Ship Could Bring Two Wars Closer
item.description:
A Ukrainian strike last weekend on an Iranian cargo ship in the Caspian Sea has underscored the links between the wars that the two countries are fighting, raising tensions between them as well as the risk of more direct confrontation.

Ukraine said the ship was carrying military equipment between Iran and Russia. Iranian officials said it was a commercial vessel, and it accused Ukraine of killing a sailor in the attack.

Iranian officials threatened retaliation in a series of statements and comments to the news media. Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, snapped back, telling Iran it had “no standing to pretend to be a victim” given its military support for Russia in its war with Ukraine.

Here’s a look at how Iran and Ukraine became adversaries through two separate wars — and why their indirect conflict now risks becoming a direct one.

Iran and Russia have had a close military relationship for decades. The most visible recent example of this is the long-range attack drones that Tehran has supplied to Moscow.

Russia launched swarms of the drones across Ukraine within months of its 2022 invasion, to deadly effect. Russia later began manufacturing its own versions of the Iranian drones.

The United States has accused Iran of supplying Russia with short-range ballistic missiles as well. And Ukraine said Iran had sent trainers to help the Russian military use drone systems, a claim that Iran denied.

The widespread use of drones, particularly the relatively cheap types provided by Iran, transformed the war in Ukraine and, more broadly, changed how military planners assess the needs of modern armies. It also forced Ukraine to develop counter-drone technologies that analysts say now rival conventional air defense systems.

Four years after Russian unleashed those Iranian drones against Ukraine, Kyiv has now brought its hard-earned expertise in countering them to the Middle East.

After the United States and Israel began their war with Iran in late February, the Iranian military launched waves of drones at U.S. military targets in Gulf countries. Ukraine saw that as an opening to showcase and export its low-cost anti-drone systems.

President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine said in March that more than 200 Ukrainian military experts had been sent to the Middle East to help defend allies against Iranian drones. “We do not want this terror of the Iranian regime against its neighbors to succeed,” he said during a speech in Britain’s Parliament.

Ukraine has also sealed defense deals with Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates focused on countering Iranian missile and drone threats.

Ukraine has increasingly portrayed its war with Russia and the war in the Middle East as intertwined, saying Iran and Russia were aiding each other in their respective conflicts.

On Saturday, Mr. Zelensky said Ukraine’s intelligence services had gathered evidence that Russia was providing Iran with satellite surveillance of Gulf states and U.S. military bases in the region, helping Tehran plan and carry out attacks. He said Ukraine would share the intelligence with its Western allies.

On the same day, Ukraine struck the Iranian ship in the Caspian Sea, accusing it of transporting military cargo between Iran and Russia, without specifying in which direction — the clearest suggestion yet that Kyiv’s long-running proxy conflict with Tehran could evolve into a more direct confrontation.

Mr. Zelensky may also use the attack to try to persuade President Trump that Ukraine and the United States share the same enemy and to advocate for closer military ties. The Ukrainian leader met with Mr. Trump on Tuesday afternoon and said the two leaders discussed securing more air defense capabilities for Kyiv.

In a post on X, Abbas Araghchi, the Iranian foreign minister, tied the attack on the ship directly to the Middle East conflict, calling the strike “a blatant U.N. Charter violation” and claiming it had been “done at Israel’s behest to drag Europe into its war.”

Mr. Araghchi added that he had spoken with both the European Union’s top diplomat and Russia’s foreign minister to make clear that the attack “CANNOT GO UNANSWERED.”

Mr. Sybiha sought to ease tensions on Tuesday, saying in a social media post that he had called Mr. Araghchi to coordinate and avoid misunderstandings. “Our position remains unchanged: Europe and the Middle East deserve stability, security, and peace,” he said.

Leily Nikounazar contributed reporting.

item.title: Iran Publicly Hangs 2 Protesters, Rights Groups Say
item.description:
The Iranian authorities publicly hanged on Tuesday two participants in the country’s widespread January protests, human rights groups said, the latest executions in what activists describe as a rapid increase in the government’s use of the death penalty this year.

The hangings were carried out at dawn in Isfahan’s Shahid Alikhani Square, according to the Washington-based Human Rights Activists News Agency, and appeared to draw a rare public backlash.

Several videos verified by The New York Times show large crowds of chanting protesters near the site. Blurry footage circulating on Telegram and social media early on Tuesday morning in Iran showed protesters around the corner from the square, chanting “shameless” and booing.

Iran has long been one of the world’s most frequent users of capital punishment, but public executions are extremely rare. Several human rights activists described Tuesday’s hangings as an escalation by a government seeking to stifle dissent after the unrest in January, particularly during the war with the United States.

Mahmood Amiry-Moghaddam, director of the Norwegian-based Iran Human Rights group, called the executions “a brutal form of state terror that the international community must not tolerate.” He said, “Public executions are among the regime’s most potent instruments for instilling fear and fostering a sense of helplessness among the public.”

The two men executed on Tuesday were Amirhossein Safari and Abolfazl Sepahi, according to Mizan, the news agency associated with Iran’s judiciary. Mizan did not mention a public execution, but two other media outlets in Iran described the hangings as being conducted “in the presence of the public.”

The men were part of a group accused by security forces of killing four police officers during protests on the night of Jan. 8. According to an indictment, the assailants attacked the officers with knives, machetes and axes, then doused them with gasoline and set their bodies on fire.

Lawyers representing the two men did not publicly comment on the charges, but both men gave televised confessions broadcast on Iran’s state news channel several months ago. Iranian rights groups and human rights lawyers say such confessions are often made under duress, frequently after psychological or physical torture.

Several human rights groups said that the men, like other protesters sentenced to death after the January demonstrations, had not been given due process.

A report released by Human Rights Activists News Agency, or HRANA, said that lawyers for Mr. Safari and Mr. Sepahi had faced difficulties gaining access to their case files and that the court rejected what could have been exculpatory evidence. The families were kept in the dark about the details of the verdicts, the report said.

According to HRANA, fourteen men have been sentenced to death on charges of involvement in the police officers’ killings, though it identified only 12 of them by name.

The selection of Shahid Alikhani Square for the execution was likely symbolic, because it is where the authorities allege that the four officers were killed, said Hassan Nayeb-Hashem, founder of the Vienna-based All Human Rights for All in Iran.

Saeid Dehghan, an Iranian human rights lawyer based in Toronto, described the event as the government “baring its teeth in an effort to suppress the public.”

Yet several videos appear to show that the hangings had the opposite effect on some people.

In one video, a crowd can be heard booing as the Islamic call to prayer rings out. Another video shows more crowds in a different area on the outskirts of Shahid Alikhani Square. In the footage, shots are heard ringing out, and the person filming begins to run.

Several Iranian-focused rights groups have warned for months that the pace of sentencing and hangings appears to have surged amid the war.

Mahya Ostovar, founder of the Iranian Democratic Diaspora Network in Ireland, said that more than 800 executions had been verified this year. “As the world’s attention has focused on war and diplomacy, the human rights catastrophe inside Iran has only intensified,” she said.

The United States and Israel launched their war against Iran just weeks after security forces crushed nationwide demonstrations. The government says some 3,000 people were killed in the protests, while activist groups like HRANA put the toll above 7,000.

“These executions should also serve as a warning that the real war in Iran has never been the one dominating international headlines,” Ms. Ostovar said. “The real conflict is the ongoing struggle between the Iranian people and the Islamic Republic. That struggle is far from over.”

item.title: France and Spain Race to Contain Fires Before Some Areas Reach 104 Degrees
item.description:
Firefighters in Spain and France were racing against the clock on Tuesday to keep ferocious wildfires near Madrid and Bordeaux in check before a scorching heat wave hits both areas, which could worsen the largest blazes the countries have faced in their modern history.

Officials in both countries welcomed an overnight respite, including rainfall and milder temperatures, which allowed firefighters to contain the spread of the fire. Some evacuees have been able to return home. But firefighters are bracing for the hours and days to come.

“It isn’t over yet, the fire is not under control,” Fabien Tuleu, an official in the southwestern Gironde area of France, repeated several times at a news conference on Tuesday. The fight, he said, “is still ongoing.”

Temperatures in parts of Spain and France are expected to climb to 104 degrees Fahrenheit, or 40 degrees Celsius, this week — the latest in a succession of extreme heat events that have parched vegetation, combining with strong winds to increase the risk of fires spreading. More than 300,000 acres have burned in Spain and France.

Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez of Spain said firefighters were “turning the tide” against the wildfires in the Madrid region and the surrounding areas. In the Madrid region alone, 20,000 people will be allowed to return to their towns, while shelter-in-place orders will be lifted for another 14,000, a regional official said.

But Mr. Sánchez warned that “difficult, critical hours” still lay ahead.

“A new heat wave will obviously hinder firefighting efforts and increase the risk of further fires across the country,” he said at news conference in Madrid on Tuesday.

The fires in both countries have consumed nearly 450 structures in France and several hundred estimated in Spain, highlighting the challenge faced by Europe as summers grow increasingly hot and wildfires become more widespread. The blazes have also tested the endurance of local residents.

In the Castellón province of Spain, where one fire is raging, Amparo Escribano, 53, was in tears on Tuesday as the Guardia Civil stopped her from getting closer to Tales, the town where she lives and had been evacuated from on Saturday.

“This is horrible,” she said, looking at flames and clouds of smoke covering the town’s bell tower in the distance. “I can’t watch this.”

The wildfire, which is north of Valencia and has scorched more than 21,000 acres in the province, remained active in some areas. Ms. Escribano fled with her parents and her son, but she left her cat behind, and authorities would not let her through to get it. She turned back toward Onda, the town where she works at a supermarket.

“I’m going to take a tranquilizer, and go to work,” she said, crying.

Flames have also come unsettlingly close to the Spanish capital and to Bordeaux, which is France’s sixth-largest city and a famed center of its wine industry. French officials said they feared that fire near Bordeaux could quickly pick up again due to an “unfavorable” weather forecast.

Sophie Brocas, the prefect for the region that includes Bordeaux, told reporters on Tuesday that evacuees from three cities in Gironde that were spared from the flames would be allowed to return, but should keep their phones on and have a bag ready in case they need to leave immediately.

Jean-Noël Schmidt, a 68 year-old magistrate, was evacuated on Friday from Andernos-les-Bains, a town west of Bordeaux, with his partner, Sylvie Blondin. She lives in Le Porge, a nearby town that suffered a disproportionate brunt of the damage: Of the 240 homes destroyed in the region, more than 180 burned there.

Ms. Blandin’s home, in one part of the town, escaped the flames on Friday, but on Tuesday they were threatening again.

“We’ve just learned that it’s far from a done deal,” Mr. Schmidt said. If the fire reaches Ms. Blandin’s neighborhood, which is dotted with wooden chalets amid a highly flammable pine forest — “everything will burn down,” he added.

Mayors of towns affected by the wildfires said the next hours would be crucial in bringing the blazes under control, as shifting weather conditions made them unpredictable.

“At night, this fire is a sleeping kitten, but during the day it becomes a huge lion,” said Fernando Casado, the mayor of Robledo de Chavela, a town west of Madrid.

France and Spain have continued to preventively evacuate people from the threatened areas. On Tuesday, about 4,000 people were evacuated from camping sites, tourist accommodations and vacation villages in Lacanau, on France’s Atlantic coast.

More than 220,000 people have been evacuated in recent days in the Gironde region. Slightly farther south, in the Landes region, 31,000 people were evacuated, but 15,000 were later allowed to return.

The Gironde blaze is the worst in France since World War II, President Emmanuel Macron of France said on Monday as he visited a local fire department and warned that the fire could take weeks to extinguish. Over 90 firefighters have been injured in the Gironde fire since it broke out on Wednesday.

More than 100,000 people in Spain were ordered to flee their homes or take shelter in recent days.

In Nules, a town north of Valencia that has taken in scores of evacuees, volunteers in blue vests were feeding hundreds of people on Monday in a local sports hall. The Serra d’Espadà mountain range rose in the distance under a haze of smoke, as firefighting seaplanes regularly flew by.

Francisco Sánchez Sabater, 49, said he had been napping at his home in Vilavella when the fire caught him by surprise. The flames were less than 200 feet away, he said.

“If the Guardia Civil hadn’t banged on my door to wake me up, they would have found me dead,” he said. Police officers told him to grab whatever he could.

“I even left my phone inside the house,” he said, describing how he ran out and walked downhill. “Every so often I’d turn around, and the smoke was already hanging over the town.”

item.title: ‘Better Chemistry’: Has the Trump-Zelensky Relationship Thawed?
item.description:
President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine met President Trump at the White House on Tuesday as their relationship appears stronger than ever before — even as both men face challenges at home.

At the meeting, Mr. Zelensky, still confronting domestic fallout over sacking both his defense minister and army chief, was hoping to reboot stalled peace talks in Ukraine’s war against Russia and to push for more U.S. help with weapons, particularly air defense. It was likely, analysts said, that the men would discuss the potential of a cease-fire in long-range airstrikes between Russia and Ukraine.

Mr. Zelensky will also attend the funeral of Senator Lindsey Graham, who died suddenly on July 11, hours after returning from Ukraine. The South Carolina Republican was perhaps Ukraine’s biggest ally in Mr. Trump’s circle, whose members have typically echoed Russian talking points.

Some analysts have speculated that Mr. Graham’s death might push Mr. Trump to be more sympathetic toward Ukraine. Some have also taken note of the visit this month to Ukraine by the right-wing activist Laura Loomer, part of the MAGA movement, who has recently expressed support for Ukraine.

Others said Mr. Trump wanted to revive peace talks because he needed a diplomatic win and because reaching a lasting cease-fire in the U.S. war on Iran has proved elusive.

“The relationship with Iran is still very much fragile,” said Harry Nedelcu, a senior director at Rasmussen Global, a European political advisory firm. So, he added, “Ukraine comes to the forefront.”

“But most importantly for both men,” he continued, “this is a moment where they could validate each other’s diplomatic efforts and leverage each other. Trump could leverage Zelensky, and Zelensky could help him validate his own administration at a time when domestically, Trump is not doing very well.”

The two leaders have long had a tricky relationship. Their meeting at the White House at the beginning of Mr. Trump’s second term was a disaster, punctuated by Mr. Zelensky’s being asked to leave. The Trump administration has consistently leaned toward Russia in peace negotiations, saying Mr. Zelensky did not have the cards to win. Under Mr. Trump, the United States cut off almost all military aid to Ukraine.

Mr. Zelensky has worked hard to mollify Mr. Trump in subsequent meetings. And Ukraine has fared better against Russia this year than expected, largely because of its drone advances. Ukraine is projecting the kind of strength that Mr. Trump typically favors.

The United States has also turned to Ukraine for help with drones and with drone interceptors, particularly in the war on Iran.

Got a confidential news tip? The New York Times would like to hear from readers who want to share messages and materials with our journalists.

“There is a better chemistry now I see between them,” said Volodymyr Dubovyk, director of the Center for International Studies at Odesa National University in Ukraine.

“Maybe Zelensky understands Trump a little better,” he added. “Maybe Trump understands Zelensky a little bit better.”

Ukraine has even peripherally entered the fray in the Iran war, hitting an Iranian ship in the Caspian Sea with a long-range drone on Saturday. Iran, which has long provided drone technology to Russia that is used against Ukraine, said the ship was a commercial vessel, vowed retaliation and accused Ukraine of deliberately widening the war. Mr. Zelensky said Kyiv had struck a cargo vessel moving military supplies between Iran and Russia.

While Ukraine’s long-range drones have also caused damage in parts of Russia, Ukraine is at a significant disadvantage in the air war. So far in July, Russia has fired 117 ballistic missiles at Ukrainian cities, according to a New York Times data set based on numbers from the Ukrainian Air Force, almost a monthly record.

Mr. Zelensky has repeatedly asked for more U.S.-made Patriot interceptor missiles — the only air defense system Ukraine possesses that is capable of shooting down Russia’s ballistic missiles. This month, in another positive sign for Ukraine, Mr. Trump agreed to allow Ukraine to produce the interceptors, although ramping up production will take years.

Ms. Loomer, who often talks to Mr. Trump, is emblematic of the shift in thinking on the war from part of Mr. Trump’s base.

Like others in the MAGA movement, she used to regularly espouse Russian talking points and oppose U.S. aid for Ukraine. But this year, Ms. Loomer said in an interview with The New York Times, she started questioning her beliefs, describing a “woke right” of influential media figures including Tucker Carlson who had swallowed Russian propaganda on Ukraine and were undermining American national security.

Last week, she made a surprise visit to Ukraine, traveling about 35 hours from her home in Florida to the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv. On Thursday, Ms. Loomer interviewed Mr. Zelensky in a garden near the presidential residence, acknowledging that she felt a moral obligation to correct the record.

Ms. Loomer, who said she had repeatedly gone to bomb shelters during air raid sirens, said on Saturday that she had called Mr. Trump twice from Ukraine.

“He said, ‘Oh, tell Zelensky I said hello,’” Ms. Loomer recounted as her team drove from the eastern city of Kharkiv to Kyiv, stopping at military checkpoints and to film a video at a bombed-out gas station.

“And then, you know, I knew that Zelensky would be at the White House next week, and Zelensky had nothing but nice things to say,” Ms. Loomer added, noting that she intended to spend another week in Ukraine visiting factories and military sites.

After she posted a preview of her interview with Mr. Zelensky online, Mr. Trump shared it on his social media site. “Very good!!!” he said.

The White House did not respond to a request for comment.

While Ms. Loomer says Mr. Trump likes both Mr. Zelensky and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia, she also says Mr. Trump realizes Mr. Putin is the problem.

“I think the tide is really changing,” she said. She added later in the interview, “I really honestly do believe that Ukraine, over time, could end up being one of our greatest allies.”

Natalia Yermak contributed reporting.
